Several people had requested after the last lecture I gave on the baptism with the Holy
Spirit on the question of who has the Holy Spirit and how fully that I would follow it
out by giving a lecture on the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
And so that is what I decided to do this evening.
Now I want to start just not by reading but by referring to the main passages in the New
Testament which speak about gifts.
There are a whole series of passages beginning with our list in Romans chapter 12, Romans
chapter 12 verse 3 through 8 where Paul commands the Christians in the Church of Rome to examine
themselves and to see what gifts they have and then to exercise them as God gives them
faith to do so.
And he gives a whole list of gifts in this passage, prophesying teaching, service, encouraging
contribution, leadership, showing mercy.
Then in 1 Corinthians 12 Paul gives two lists.
The first in verses 4, down through 11 he gives a list of various gifts of wisdom and
knowledge, faith, healing, miraculous powers, prophecy, discernment, speaking tongues, interpretation.
And then later on in 1 Corinthians 12 in verses 27 through 31 Paul gives another list of gifts
where he speaks of apostles, prophets, teachers, workers of miracles, healing, help, helps
administration and tongues and interpretation he mentions further down.
And it's interesting that you have two passages in the same chapter where Paul doesn't just
repeat the same gifts, he repeats a rather different gift of this the second time, some
which are the same as the first list, the others are different.
You have another list in Ephesians 4 where the emphasis is a little different.
In the passages we've looked at Paul speaks about the gifts God gives to people.
In the passage in Ephesians 4 he speaks about people as gifts which Christ gives to the
church.
Ephesians chapter 4 verse 11 verses 11 and 12 and 13 Paul speaks about gifts given to
the church, apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers.
And then there's another short statement about gifts in 1 Peter chapter 4 verse 10.
Now from these lists of gifts it's obvious that we're dealing with a big question that
there's all sorts of gifts which the New Testament refers to, I haven't given the whole list,
but it obviously isn't intended to be exhaustive because every time a list is given different
gifts occur.
As we think about this what is the place of these gifts of the Holy Spirit today, both
those mentioned in the New Testament and all sorts of others because some of the gifts
mentioned to serve very general, they clearly include many, many things like gifts of service
or gifts of helps for each of those we could think of many, many things which they would
include.
So we have a huge list of gifts that we're dealing with.
As we think about these gifts I want to try to get at some issues involved in the gifts
of the Holy Spirit and their place in the church today by asking a series of questions.
And I've thought about these questions as a means of getting at the debate that goes
on in the church at the moment about the place of the gifts of the Spirit.
The first is this, are gifts a measure of spirituality, are gifts a measure of spirituality, are
gifts a measure of the fullness of the Spirit in an individual's life or the power of the
Holy Spirit.
Now this is an important question to ask because there are many people in the church
who teach that they are and we talked a little bit about this last time when we were speaking
about the baptism of the Spirit that there are sections of the church which teach that
there are two stages in the Christian life and that the second stage of a greater power
of the Spirit or a greater fullness of the Spirit is shown by the receiving of particular
gifts from the Holy Spirit.
Very often the gift of tongues is seen as the mark that one has entered into a greater
depth of relationship with the Holy Spirit and new power, a power to be a witness or whatever.
Others would say there must be specific gifts, it might not necessarily be the gift of tongues.
But the heart of the idea is that there are two stages of the Christian life, one woman
is converted, one perhaps, years later, maybe only a short time later, maybe right after
conversion, where one receives the Holy Spirit in much greater fullness and this is evidenced
by the exercise of particular gifts and very often the gifts which are picked out are those
which are more, perhaps we say, unusual gifts like tongues or more unusual in their manifestation.
So this is an important problem and because in this context where this is taught, questions
will then be encouraged to say do you have this particular gift if you had this particular
gift then you would know that you had a full relationship with the Holy Spirit, then you
could be sure you have the Spirit's power in your life.
So it's an important question but we have to say if we're asking that question, our gift
is a measure of spirituality, a measure of Christian maturity, the New Testament quite
clearly says no, gifts may certainly have their place and we'll come to that later the
positive place of gifts in the church but they're clearly not seen as a measure of spirituality
in the New Testament.
We can look at 1 Corinthians 1, 1 Corinthians chapter 1, 1 Corinthians of course is the
letter about which most in which most is said about the gifts of the Spirit in the New Testament
but Paul in 1 Corinthians chapter 1 verse 7 says, "Therefore you do not lack any spiritual
gift as you eagerly wait for our Lord Jesus Christ to be revealed."
This is his comment on the Corinthian church, you don't lack any spiritual gift.
There's a church where there are many gifts received and being exercised in the church.
However, he makes the comment in chapter 3, verse 1, even though this is the case, even
though the church is full of spiritual gifts, he says, "Brothers, I could not address you
as spiritual but as worldly, mere infants in Christ.
I gave you milk, not solid food, for you are not yet ready for it.
Indeed you are still not ready, you are still worldly, but since there is jealousy and quarrelling
among you, are you not worldly?
Are you not acting like mere men?"
And then Paul goes on to speak about their divisions.
So Paul is saying, "Despite the fact that you have all these gifts far from being spiritual,
you are the opposite, you're just acting like everybody else had in the world, having
divisions among yourselves fighting and bickering about all sorts of things, one group following
this leader, another group following that leader."
And in 1st Corinthians 13, Paul gives us what he calls the most excellent way, the last verse
of chapter 12.
And now I will show you the most excellent way, where Paul makes it clear that what must
be essential in the Christian life is not the gifts that one has but love.
And that is the measure of the Christian's maturity.
He says, "If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only
a resounding gonger of clamming, plain symbol; if I have the gift of prophecy, I can fathom
all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have a face that can move mountains but have
not love, I am nothing; and if I give all I possess to the poor, and surrender my body
to the flames but have not love, I gain nothing."
So Paul picking on both a more dramatic gift, if you like, like tongues, and then the gift
of service of oneself, giving oneself to other people, giving away everything one has, the
gift of contribution as he refers to it in Romans.
And he says, "In both cases, you can do all these things.
You can exercise these gifts, but if you don't have love, then you're nothing."
So that what is central, the measure of a Christian's maturity, is not what particular
gifts they have, necessarily, but rather their love, their commitment to really care for other
people in response to the love of God for them.
So that's the first thing.
We have to say that gifts are not necessarily a measure of spirituality or of the power
of the Spirit in a person's life.
As Paul says, it's quite possible to have all sorts of different gifts of teaching or
whatever, and if one is without love, then one is getting nowhere.
That brings us to a second question, which we can ask, and that is, is spiritual power
exhibited in gifts a sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit, necessarily?
Is spiritual power exhibited in gifts a sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit, necessarily?
Again I ask this question because there are some people today who have taught that if
we see people exercising certain gifts, then that must mean the Holy Spirit is present.
I always remember a quite well-known now article in Crusade magazine several years ago when
one charismatic leader was saying this.
He was saying, "We look at the Roman Catholic Church, and we look at the liberal church,
and we see people in these groups exercising certain gifts of the Spirit, exercising the
gifts that we see among ourselves, the gifts of tongues, prophecy, healing, and so on.
Therefore he says, "Since we are exercising the same gifts, therefore we can get together
because this is evidence that the same Spirit is working."
Now that may of course may have been so in the particular circumstance, but the New Testament
doesn't see that as being a necessary basis on which one can draw the conclusion that
the Holy Spirit is working in somebody's life, that one sees certain manifestations in their
life.
Rather it asks some other questions, and we could just look at a couple of passages.
First John chapter 4, where that's towards the end of the New Testament, if you've got
a new international verse in page 297, verse John chapter 4 verse 1, and John puts this
to the people in the church.
He says, "Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether
they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world."
Now how does John say that to be tested, not by the fact that they prophesy, or that they
have some spiritual manifestation, the test he gives is a doctrinal test.
He says, "Do they acknowledge that Jesus is the Christ who came in the flesh?"
In other words, a very particular doctrinal test was the test of whether the spirit is
present is not a particular manifestation, but the truth of the doctrine.
We've had the first test of maturity as love, the second of the presence of the spirit must
be truth, must be truth, 1 John 4 verses 1 through 3, and the same sort of thing in Galatians
chapter 1 verses 8 through 9, Galatians 1 verse 8 and 9, where Paul writing to the Galatians
church is stressing the importance of the gospel that he's preached of salvation through faith
in Christ alone.
And in the Galatian church, there has been the problem that some people have been coming
along and teaching the Christians that as well as believing in Christ, they must be circumcised
in order to be saved and they must observe certain other works, certain other practices.
And Paul says, in this context, he says, verse 8, "But even if we are an angel from heaven
should preach a gospel other than the one we have preached to you, let him be eternally
condemned."
As we have already said, so now I say again, if anybody is preaching to your gospel other
than that, what you accepted, let him be eternally condemned.
In other words, again Paul says, "It's not the power or the manifestation with which
a person comes which is the final test of whether they're coming with the Spirit of
God.
The test is a doctrinal one.
Do they preach the same gospel that Paul preached?"
And another kind of similar passage, though not stated so strongly in a rather different
context, 1 Corinthians 14 verse 37 and 38.
Paul says, "If anybody thinks he's a prophet or spiritually gifted, let him acknowledge
that what I am writing to you is the Lord's command.
If he ignores this, he himself will be ignored."
And again, Paul here among Christians now, in this context, gives a statement here that
the test, the test of whether somebody's prophecy or spiritual gift is genuine is whether they
acknowledge the authority of Paul and we could say the other apostles, whether they obey
the teaching of the apostles.
So the second test then, we've had the first as love as the measure of spirituality.
The test of whether someone comes from the Holy Spirit or with the power of the Spirit
is not what manifestation or what gift they express, but rather the truth that they're
teaching the truth of the apostolic message.
Now in this particular article in Crusades I referred to earlier, the person who wrote
it went on to say, "Because these people have the same gifts, therefore we can get together."
He went on to say, "Evangelicals in the past have made the mistake of insisting that people
get together on the basis of shared truth.
But now we know that we can get together on the basis of shared gifts."
And it's against that that these passages we're looking at as speaking here, it says
we must get together and recognize the Spirit on the basis of the truth that is taught, not
necessarily a gift that is exercised because it's possible for the gifts of the Holy Spirit
of whatever kind to be can't have peated, to be can't have peated, either by just simply
human emotion and human ability or by demonic power.
So that's the second thing, that the test of the presence of the Spirit is the truth
of the apostolic doctrine being present.
Thirdly, the third question, are gifts the primary guarantee that I have the Spirit or
that I belong to Christ?
And in a way this is related to the first question, are gifts the primary guarantee that I have
the Spirit or that I belong to Christ, i.e. are the gifts that I have, the source of my
assurance of my status before God?
Now again I ask this question because some teach that they are, I've had people say to
me many times, if you really want to know that you have the Holy Spirit, if you really
want to know that you belong to Christ, why don't you exercise this particular gift or
that particular gift?
In other words, if you really want assurance that you have a personal relationship with
God, then you ought to exercise such and such a gift.
Now clearly one has to respond to that, no, gifts are not the primary guarantee that I
have the Spirit of God or that I have fellowship with Christ.
You can think of Jesus' words in Luke's Gospel to his disciples where he said, you
remember the disciples came to Jesus after he had sent them out to preach and to heal
and to cast out demons and they came back and they done these things and they were really
excited and they were rejoicing about it.
And Jesus says, yes, I saw late Satan falling like lightning from heaven and then he went
on to say, but do not rejoice in those things, rejoice that your names are written in heaven.
And what he's saying is that while gifts and wonderful things in our lives, wonderful
things that we see God do through us, through the gifts we may have, in this case it was
healing and casting out of demons, while these are wonderful things and have their place,
what are rejoicing, most rest upon is God's love for us expressed in Christ that our names
are written in heaven.
And that's where our source of assurance must come and we can think of the way Paul writes
in Colossians chapter 2 where he's talking there about Christian fullness, Colossians
chapter 2 verses 6 and 10, he says, so then just as you receive Christ Jesus' Lord continue
to live in him, rooted and built up in him, strengthened in the faith as you were taught
in overflowing with thankfulness.
In verse 10 you have been given fullness in Christ and with Paul stressing that the center
of our lives as Christians and the center of our confidence before God must not be any
particular gift that we have, but rather Christ and all he has done for us on the cross.
And the salvation we have through him, Colossians 2 verses 6 and 10 and of course there are
many other passages which say the same thing, you can think of Hebrews chapter 12 verse 2
where the writer of Hebrews speaks, he says, that is spix our eyes on Jesus, the author
and perfecter of our faith, that is spix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of
our faith, in other words that our confidence and the source of our growth fundamentally
is not in a particular gift that we have but rather in Christ who has both begun our faith,
he's the author of it and he's the one who's going to make it perfect, he's going to complete
it, that would be the third thing, so that gifts are not then the primary guarantee that
I have the spirit or that I belong to Christ, rather it is Christ himself who must be at
the center of my life.
And fourthly we can ask another question, is there a hierarchy or should there be seen
to be a hierarchy of gifts between natural and supernatural ordinary and extraordinary
and what we could call human and obviously from the spirit?
Should there be a hierarchy of gifts between natural and supernatural gifts, ordinary and
extraordinary gifts and so on?
And again we have to respond to that question, no there shouldn't be, there should not be
seen to be a hierarchy of gifts between natural, supernatural, ordinary and extraordinary.
You can think of the lists in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12, it's quite clear when you
look at them that both lists include gifts which are normally considered to be ordinary
and extraordinary, tongues, prophecy, healing, showing mercy, serving, contributing, ruling,
governing, works of miracles, faith, healing, interpretation, discernment of spirits.
Now Paul just gives these lists just any odd how in a way.
He doesn't single add the more extraordinary ones or the less extraordinary ones as being
more important than the others, so you see no sort of hierarchy made between those gifts
which are more obviously from God, more obviously directly the work of the spirit than those
which seem to be more natural.
And I think that we have a problem sometimes in discussions about gifts because some groups
tend to see only the more extraordinary gifts, gifts like tongues and interpretation, healing,
performing miracles, discerning spirits, casting out of spirits and so on prophecy as
they understand it.
Some groups tend to see only those gifts as being the gifts that are really spiritual or
there are really evidences of the spirit's power.
Now the problem with such a view, the problem with such a view is that it's a too narrow
view of the Holy Spirit's work, it's a too narrow view of the Holy Spirit's work because
it tends to see only those gifts which are more unusual or if you like are more obviously
directly from God, it tends to see only those as being really the work of the spirit.
And whereas in the New Testament it's made quite clear that all the gifts including most
mundane gifts of administration or service or whatever are seen as equally to be charismatic
gifts, grace gifts given by God to the church.
I think the fundamental problem with the view is we were talking about this in another context
the other day is that some Christians can have the desire to walk by sight rather than
by faith so that then the obvious manifestations of the spirit's presence like tongues or healing
or casting out demons or slaying in the spirit or whatever, though that isn't mentioned
in the New Testament and we could talk about that later, that those more obvious manifestations
of the spirit's presence are seem to be the more valuable because they assure me that
the Holy Spirit is working in my life.
But the New Testament says we walk by faith and not by sight and that we don't have to
depend upon things being more obvious to have confidence that the Holy Spirit is working
in our lives.
Sometimes the spirit does work in more dramatic ways, but Jesus describes his work in John
3 as a secret work, so as the spirit's work as a secret work is like the wind, you see
the wind's effects, you don't see where the wind has come from or where it's going, you
see the consequences of the spirit's work.
So when we look at gifts like administration or showing mercy or visiting a sick or teaching,
and in such gifts there is obvious human effort involved by the person who exercises the gift
of administration or teaching or showing mercy, we must see those gifts where human effort
is clearly involved as being just as much demonstrations of the spirit's gifting and
power, just as much demonstrations of the spirit's gifting and power as we would view
the more dramatic gifts like tongues or healing or whatever because that is the attitude of
the New Testament, it doesn't differentiate between the gifts in this way and set up this
kind of hierarchy, now that leads me to another point and that is it's clear from the New
Testament that there must be no barrier set up between human effort and spiritual gift,
the gift of the spirit, there must be no barrier set up between human effort and spiritual
gift, I remember hearing a talk once where somebody suggested that there were different
things that were the spirit's gifts and then there were natural abilities or talents that
we have and that the two should be rigidly differentiated because the gifts that the
spirit gave were ones that were exercised apart from human effort and human learning
whereas our talents and so on were exercised by our effort.
Now the New Testament never makes that kind of division or distinction or sets a barrier
between the two like that and again you see all these gifts put together so James can
write, he says let not many of you be teachers because you'll be judged with greater strictness
or Paul can write to Timothy pay attention to what you teach, pay attention to what you
teach, be careful about what you teach, in other words Paul clearly speaks to Timothy
that he's got all sorts of gifts, he tells him so, he says exercise the gifts that were
given to you, the laying on of hands of the Presbyterian but then he goes on to say pay
attention to what you teach, in other words we shouldn't see it set a pull apart the effort
that we put into exercising a gift and our confidence that the Holy Spirit has both given
us the gift and it's going to exercise his power through us in our as we exercise this
gift for myself I would say in preparing a sermon that my calling before God is to work
hard to understand a particular passage or a particular idea, to think of that ways to
communicate it which will make it come across to the people who are listening, it will be
helpful to them to think about their needs, my own needs and to try and apply the word
of God, that is my responsibility before God to do that yet at the same time I would say
I think I have some sort of a gift of teaching from the Holy Spirit and I pray that the Holy
Spirit will help me as I'm doing that preparation and we mustn't see the two things as opposed
to each other, I'm not able to look into my mind and see exactly how the Spirit works
or where he helps me to know what to say or gives me a wisdom about the needs of the
people I'm going to be speaking to but I don't even understand and I can only see afterwards
as I look back and somebody comes to me and says thank you for saying such a thing and
it was so helpful because I was struggling with this particular problem and I maybe didn't
know they were struggling with the problem at all but over and over again one sees that
if one prays for the Spirit to lead one and to help one as when exercises whatever gifts
one gives one's given one sees in wonderful ways the way he works secretly into one's
experience in a way that one cannot touch and look at but one can look back and say yes
I can clearly see how the Spirit has led me so then we must never make that division
between human effort and the power and work of the Spirit in a gift you can think of the
way Paul sums this up in 1st Corinthians 15 verse 10 he says I worked harder than any
of them yet not I but the grace of God that was in me and you see Paul putting these two
things together I worked harder than any of them yet not I but the grace of God that was
in 1st Corinthians 15 verse 10. Now fifthly that brings us to another question
our gifts for today are gifts for today in the church should gifts be exercised in the
church today now why do I ask that question it seems rather obvious that gifts are for
today but the question arises because some people teach that the spiritual gifts the charismatic
gifts finished with the age of the apostles finished with the age of the apostles that
when the last apostle died the spiritual gifts died out the charismatic gifts died out in
the church they would argue that these gifts were only given for the setting up of the church
through the ministry of the apostles and that when their ministry was finished then the
gifts passed away and they would argue on that basis that then the gift of tongues is
a legitimate today and so on and then many of these other gifts as well. Now on what
basis would they argue such a thing the appeal is usually made to 1st Corinthians chapter
13 1st Corinthians chapter 13 and the appeal is made to these verses verses 8 through 12
this is love never fails but whether it prophecies they will cease whether it tongues they will
be stilled whether it's knowledge it will pass away for we know in part and we prophesy
in part but when perfection comes the imperfect disappears and so on now some people interpret
that passage as saying that tongues and prophecy and so on will pass away love will remain
but tongues and prophecy will pass away when the perfect comes and they interpret the perfect
as being the end of the apostolic age the giving of the whole New Testament. Now if you look
further down the passage it's quite clear that it's talking about the believer standing
before the Lord he goes on to speak about same Christ face to face and being fully known
by him in other words it's not talking at all about the end of the apostolic age it's
talking quite clearly about the believer's going to be with the Lord that's what the
perfection is that Paul is referring to this passage can't possibly be used to support
the idea that spiritual gifts ceased with the apostolic age or with the finishing of
the New Testament as if therefore gifts were no longer needed. The other problem with this
position apart from the fact that it can't be defended from the New Testament the other
problem with the position is that it proves too much if you try to say the charismatic
gifts ceased with the age of the apostles because the New Testament does not distinguish
between let's say extraordinary and ordinary gifts if one says they ceased with the apostolic
age when it has to say that all ordinary gifts ceased with the apostolic age too and that
gifts of teaching and administration and so on ceased as well which obviously causes
a problem because Paul uses the term charisma to refer to all of these gifts. The teaching
is just as much a charismatic gift as prophecy, administration is just as much a gift as tons.
So the argument in which proves too much because nobody would want to argue that there were
no gifts in the church today. However, the one thing that can be said for this view I
don't agree with it but the one thing can be said in terms of a slight sort of approval
for one point of it is this that Paul does speak of the signs of an apostle in 2 Corinthians
chapter 12, 2 Corinthians chapter 12 verse 12. He says the things that mark an apostle
signs, wonders and miracles were done among you with great perseverance. The things that
mark an apostle signs, wonders and miracles were done among you with great perseverance.
In other words Paul is clearly saying that Christ authenticated his apostolic calling
a ministry by pouring out these special gifts on Paul's ministry, these special signs of
miracles and healing and so on. In Paul's ministry and we quite clearly see that if you
look through the book of Acts Paul did a great number of healings. It says that even when
it speaks about the apostles that even when their shadow passed by people were healed.
So you have some very dramatic healings and on a very wide scale in the ministry of the
apostles and Paul sees those things as the signs which mark an apostles ministry. And
we would have to say in commenting on that this that in God's dealing with man, in God's
dealing with man there are particular times in history when there are extraordinary outpourings
of the Spirit's power, that there are particular moments in history when there are extraordinary
outpourings of the Spirit's power. Now there are two in Scripture that are given to us.
In the past the first is the Exodus, the second is the ministry of Christ and the apostles.
But as we look at the Scripture we see an extraordinary clustering of the miraculous,
of miraculous signs and wonders around those two major events in the history of redemption,
the bringing of the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt and taking them into the
promised land of Israel and then the work of Christ. That as we look at the ministry
of Moses in bringing the people of that of Egypt you have a tremendous outpouring of
signs of God's power at that time. And there is nothing like it in the rest of the Old
Testament. There you have individual miracles here and there throughout the Old Testament.
You have occasional signs and wonders which God does for his people. But there is nothing
like again what happened in the time of Moses in order with the same degree, the same number
of signs. Now again if we look back to the foundation of the church and the ministry
of Christ and the apostles we see the same thing. But as you look in the gospels something
took place which has never taken place since and it doesn't matter what anybody says about
it has certainly never taken place since. But over and over again it tells you in the
gospels and we could turn to the pastures it isn't really necessary. But it says Christ
went into a town and they brought to him everybody who was sick in the whole district with every
kind of disease and he healed all of them and it says it over and over again. Christ must
have healed thousands and thousands of people of every kind of disease. And it says this
many many times in the gospels and it's not just exaggerating because those miracles in
Jesus ministry are seen to be signs of the Kingdom of God, signs of the coming Kingdom
that will one day feel the whole earth when Christ returns when all sickness will be removed
and all death will be conquered and the power of Satan will be completely removed from the
earth. Now so you have an extraordinary outpouring of the miraculous in Christ's ministry which
has never been seen since in the history of a church. Now you have groups which claim
to have many miracles but I've never met anybody who claims to have the same degree of miracles
that you see on pages of the New Testament and certainly nobody could ever authenticate
any such thing. There are people who claim to have extraordinary gifts of healing today
and they claim that we are able to do even greater works than Christ did and they appeal
to the passage in John's gospel to defend that, that we ought to be able to do more
healings that Christ did and they say they're able to do that but if they really can do
that they ought to go into the hospitals and heal the people who are really sick and if
they don't then I'd say they're lacking compassion if they really have that gift because that
was what Christ did. They bought him everybody who was sick and he healed them. Now what
we see throughout history is that God does perform miracles and signs. God does perform
miracles and signs but there is a tremendous outpouring of miracles and particular moments
in history that's so in the Old Testament and it's so from the time of the work of Christ
until today. Now I've seen one or two healings in my ministry and I know other churches both
charismatic and non-charismatic or what are normally called such where there have been
one or two healings but nowhere have I seen any real evidence that I've seen authenticated
of tremendously huge numbers of miracles in the same degree that you find in the New
Testament. So that is the thing that can be said for this issue about the extraordinary
that we do not see the gifts of healing and miracles manifested in the same way in the
church today that you see it manifested in the New Testament. You don't see it in any
church anywhere to the same degree. We see some. We see some amazing answers to prayer.
We see people healed occasionally but not to the same degree. Now sixthly, but again
as I said that doesn't touch the question of gifts because clearly from the New Testament
the gifts are given for the whole history of the church. We may not see such a degree
of the miracles of healing and so on today as we do in the New Testament. Sixthly then
what is the purpose of the gifts? What is the purpose of the gifts? Why has God given
gifts to the church? And the answer of course is simply the up building of the church. The
up building of the church. And as we think about this, a couple of important things to
say. First of all, that when we become Christians we are saved as individuals. Each one of us
has to come to faith in Christ and come into personal fellowship with them. We are saved
as individuals. However, we are not saved to have simply an individual relationship with
God. We are saved to be a part of the body of Christ, to be a part of the fellowship
of the church. And the New Testament says this very strongly. I think of 1 Corinthians chapter
12 verses 12 and 13. 1 Corinthians 12 verses 12 and 13. Paul says the body is a unit though
it is made up of many parts and though all its parts are many, they form one body. So
it is with Christ. For we were all baptized with one spirit into one body, whether Jews
or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given the one spirit to drink. Now Paul speaks
of us that as all being baptized by the Spirit in other words, we are given the Spirit among
other things to make us a part of the body of Christ. We are given the Spirit for all
sorts of reasons to seal us as belonging to God, to give us power for our lives to be
changed, to be sanctified. But we are also given the Holy Spirit to make us a part of
the body of Christ. And no Christian should think of themselves as being simply an isolated
individual who has their own private relationship with God and that is all there is to their
Christian life. Because the New Testament makes it very plain that every Christian is called
into by virtue of their conversion and the giving of the Spirit to them, fellowship in
the body of Christ. And the New Testament sees as one of the wonders of the gospel, one
of the mysteries of the gospel, which make men marvel at it, that it takes people from
different backgrounds, racially, culturally, socially, and puts them together in the church.
I think of the way Paul prefers it in that passage there in 1 Corinthians 12, 13, where
he says, "You are all baptized into the one body, whether Jews or Greeks, people who hated
each other. Slaves are free, people who had nothing to do with each other socially and
culturally." It says the same thing in Colossians 3 verses 9 and 10. He speaks about this being
brought into the one new man, Christ, whether Jews or Greeks, barbarian or Scythians, slave
or free. Christ is all and is in all. Again, his emphasis is on when we become Christians,
we are brought into a group a new living entity of people. We're brought into a new living
entity of people who are called to give to each other and to share with each other. Christ
intends for every one of us to be receiving and giving responsible member of his church,
both in the world wide sense that every Christian belongs to the church of Christ, simply by
virtue of being a Christian, but also in the local sense that every Christian is called
to be part of a local church and to be receiving and giving within it. We are called into fellowship
with Christ, but also into the fellowship of Christ with one another. So whether we like
it or not, and maybe some of us don't like it very much, when we first become Christians,
whether we like it or not, we're called to take an active part in the church. And it
is in this context that each of us are given the gifts of the Holy Spirit that we might
be gifts ourselves to other people, to the church. That of course is the emphasis in
Ephesians 4 that God gives us as gifts to the church, to build the church. We are given
gifts to use for serving other people. So if we ask, "What is the purpose of gifts?"
The primary purpose of gifts is to serve one another in the body of Christ. A secondary
purpose would be the edification of oneself, because obviously it's an encouragement to
every individual to see their gift being exercised. It's another reason for rejoicing in the
goodness of the Lord, as one sees his work in one's life. But the primary purpose of
a gift is serving one another, serving one another. That brings us to the seventh question.
Do we all have the same gifts? Or should we all expect to have the same gifts? And again,
as we look at the New Testament, we have to answer that question quite clearly now. If
you look at 1 Corinthians 12, the whole emphasis of the passage is that God has given different
gifts to everybody in the church. Different gifts. 1 Corinthians 12 verse 4, there are
different kinds of gifts at the same spirit. There are different kinds of service for the
same Lord. There are different kinds of working with the same God works all of them in all
men. And then he goes on to give a list of some of the gifts. And verse 14, he deals with
this very question. Now the body is not made up of one part, but of many. And he talks
about the importance of there being different gifts in the church. And he talks about the
importance of there being different gifts in the church. And he, in fact, asks the question
down at the end, in verse 29, "Are all apostles, are all prophets, are all teachers, do all
work miracles, do all have gifts of healing, do all speak in tongues, do all interpret."
And all of those questions in the Greek are asked with the expectation of the answer "No."
In other words, we clearly all have different gifts. The whole point of the gift of the
spirit is that they are different because there are all sorts of needs in a local church and
therefore different gifts are given to the different members so that they'll be neutral
up building of all and all the needs that the body will be met. That brings us to an
eighth question. What should our own attitude be towards gifts? What should my attitude
be? What should your attitude be towards gifts?
First of all, Romans 12, Romans 12 verse 3. Paul says, "For by the grace given to me I
say to every one of you, do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think
of yourself with sober judgment in accordance with the measure of faith God has given you."
So Paul calls us first of all to come to a sober estimate of the place God has given
us in the body of Christ. The sober estimate of the gifts we have and the way each of us
can use our gifts in the church. That's our first thing. We come to a sober estimate
as serious and careful estimate of the gifts we have. Of course, there are two problems.
Some people can overvalue their gifts and think they've got all kinds of gifts which
they don't have. Other people can undervalue them and say, "Well, I don't have any gifts
at all and there's nothing I can do." Now Paul denies that and he says, "To everybody
is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good." We just read that in
1 Corinthians 12, "That everybody has gifts which the Holy Spirit has given them to use
in the church." So it's not a question of asking, "Do I have any gifts?" But rather,
what gifts do I have? What gifts do I have and how can I use them? And that has to be
our attitude. And in a way, it's more helpful usually for us, I think, as individuals not
to spend an enormous amount of time looking at ourselves and saying, "What am I gifts?
What am I gifts? Do I have this or do I have that?" There is some value in doing that obviously,
but because so many of us are very introspective and that's not very helpful to look at ourselves
for too long because we begin to become rather confused about what we have at all. It's often
rather more helpful to actually look at the church and see what its needs are and then
see what can I do? What can I do to meet those needs? What are the needs that are not being
met and can I help to meet them? And it's often much easier to come to a sober estimate
of our place in the body of Christ when we do that, say, "What are the needs and can
I do something about them? Can I try to help here or there?" Or wherever.
One question that's involved here is this, that we shouldn't ask. Now, if I'm asking
about what gifts I have or what I can do, the question of whether I had any ability to
do a particular thing before I became a Christian or only sins is an irrelevant question. Sometimes
people teach that only things that one becomes able to do after conversion are gifts which
the spirit can use in the church. Other things are human talents and they have no place.
But that is an irrelevant question because it denies the sovereignty of God over our
whole lives. Because God doesn't begin to be concerned with us at the moment we're converted.
As God said to Jeremiah, "I called you from the womb for this task of being a prophet
over the nations." The words that God prepared Jeremiah from his birth, from his conception
in the womb, for the particular task that God was going to give him in his church later
on. And it's the same for every one of us. The sovereignty of God is exercised in our
lives throughout our lives and God can take who we are and the training we've had and
then use us and give us new gifts after conversion and then use us to be what he wants us to
be in the church today. So it's an irrelevant question to ask, "What could I do before
I became a Christian if I could do it then I mustn't do that now?" So if one had, let's
say, some ability in teaching before him was converted, one doesn't say, "Well, I can't
teach now because that can't be a gift of the Holy Spirit." That is really an irrelevant
question because it denies the sovereignty of God. You can think of Paul, for example,
it's quite clear that God was able to use his training as a Pharisee taught by Gomeliel
when Paul was converted. Paul immediately went out and was able to preach the gospel
with a tremendously good knowledge of the Old Testament. He didn't have to deny what
he knew before. He was able to build on it. So our calling is to look at the church and
see the needs there and then see what we can do. And the fundamental thing here when we're
thinking about gifts and our own relationship to gifts is this, that we are to see ourselves
as servants. Not to see ourselves as saying, "Oh, I hope I have this particular gift or
that particular gift so that everybody can think well of me and I'll have a high place
in the church." Our attitude has to be is my calling is to be a servant. Just as Christ
said, He said, "I came not to be served, but to serve." And that is every Christian
calling in the church. Now what can I do that will impress people, but what can I do that
will serve people, whatever it is, whatever it is, whether it's something which everybody
notices. And Paul talks about that too in 1 Corinthians 12. He says, "The gifts in fact,
which nobody notices like parts of the body which you hide away are in fact the most important."
And that's something we all need to rediscover in the church to really value those things
which people don't usually bother to praise or to notice and see them as being really
important in the life of the church. So the question I'm to ask myself is always, "How
may I serve the fellowship of God's Son?" And this must involve openness too. Openness
to receiving whatever gifts God decides to give us and praying for God to give us gifts
too that we may exercise our calling more fully. So real openness before the Lord of
saying, "Lord you give me and you help me to exercise these gifts." Now that brings
us to a final question, a final question, and that is what about two particular gifts
today? And that is the gift of apostles and the gift of prophets. And here I think we
come to a rather more difficult question. First of all, the question of apostles, first
of all the question of apostles, that I think first of all we have to say that as you look
at the New Testament the authority of the apostles who were then is clearly unrepeatable.
And this is a problem because there are some people who claim to be apostles today. There
are quite a few churches, an increasing number in fact, where the group claims that it's
leaders are apostles. And in several cases there have been men who have designated themselves
as a group as apostles. It was a little book published about 15 years ago in the States
called 20th Century Appostleship, written by a man who with a group of other men formed
themselves as a group of apostles over the churches. So this is an important question.
But as we look at the New Testament I think it's clear that the authority of the apostles
was unrepeatable. First of all, in 1 Corinthians 15 verse 8 Paul describes himself as the least
of the apostles, the last of the apostles, one born out of due time. One born out of
due time. Now why did Paul write of himself in that way? The reason he wrote that way
that he was an apostle born out of due time, born after the normal time in other words,
he wasn't born at the normal time as an apostle. He says that because it was required of an
apostle that they had been with Christ during his earthly ministry and that they should
be a witness of the resurrection. And Paul called himself an apostle born out of due time
because he had not been with Christ during his earthly ministry. We see this from Acts
chapter 1. Acts chapter 1 verse 17, 21 and 22. When Judas had killed himself Peter called
the other apostles together and he said now we must replace Judas with someone else.
And the requirement for an apostle, for the one they replaced him with was precisely that
that the individual had been with Christ during his earthly ministry and then was a witness
of the resurrection also. Peter says this, he says, "One of the men who have been with
us the whole time the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from John's baptism
to the time when Jesus was taken up from us, he must be set aside for this ministry and
one of these must become with us the witness of his resurrection." It was on the basis
of those criteria that Joseph Bar-Sabbas and Matthias were put forward and then God's
choice was made known by the drawing of laws about them. So those were the two requirements
for an apostle and Paul calls himself an apostle born at a few times because the first of those
was not true with him and Paul had not been with Christ during his ministry. Only one
of the criteria was true of Paul. He was a witness of the resurrection because Christ
made a special appearance to him on the Damascus road to appoint him as an apostle and Paul
refers to that. It's referred to in Acts 9 verses 1 through 6 and verse 15 Acts 22 verses
6 through 15 and 26, 13 through 18. Each of these passages describe Paul's being appointed
as an apostle by Christ when Christ appeared to him on the Damascus road. This appearance
after the other resurrection appearances Christ makes a special appearance to Paul to appoint
him as an apostle to the Gentiles. So only one of the criteria was true of Paul and it
was because that was so that only one of those criteria was true of Paul. Paul was always
in the position of having to defend his apostleship, both in the letters to the Corinthians and
in the Galatian church Paul was in the position of having to defend his apostleship because
he had been born out of due time. He was continually having to argue that his apostleship wasn't
a secondary apostleship, that he wasn't an apostle appointed by other men, but rather
he was an apostle appointed directly by Christ. You can think of his words in Galatians 1
verses 11 through 12, 15 through 17 and then the same in 2 Corinthians. In all of these
passages Paul has to argue that he's a genuine apostle who's been directly appointed by Christ
because there were many people who attacked him presumably partly because he hadn't been
with Christ during his ministry. Now the question then arises if Paul was born out of due time
and could be an apostle could not there be other apostles since Paul's time and let's
say today who are also born out of due time. Now that seems to be directly denied I should
suggest when Paul calls himself the last of the apostles 1 Corinthians 15 verse 8. And
we have another problem, even if somebody does claim to be an apostle today and claims
to be a witness of the resurrection, which would seem to be necessary, even if someone
did claim to be an apostle today and claim to be a witness of the resurrection, there
would still be some problems. How could their claim to be appointed by Christ be supported?
And this is where Paul was in a unique position because even though he was born out of due
time, the other apostles recognized his claim to be appointed by Christ and Paul refers to
this. While he makes a point of saying I wasn't appointed by men, Christ appointed me directly,
he also says the other apostles extended to me the right hand of fellowship. That's
in Galatians chapter 2, Paul refers to that. He says they accepted his fellowship, Galatians
1 18, 19, 24 and chapter 2 verses 2 and 6 through 9. So Paul's authority was unique because
he lived at the same time as the other apostles. And you have in the New Testament places where
the other apostles refer to Paul as an apostle. You can think of Peter's letter, 2 Peter 3
15 to 16, where Peter refers to Paul's writings as scripture, as being the word of God. In
other words, Peter clearly recognizes Paul's authority. The problem with somebody claiming
apostolic authority today is that there can't any longer be in a position where their claim
can be supported by the other apostles. In other words, in a way they're on their own
and it's only they themselves who can insist that they must be apostles. Now, some would
then maybe argue, but the word apostle itself simply means a missionary. Somebody sent out.
Why can't we use the word apostle today? And why can't we have sort of apostolic delegates
in the church today? You have responsibility over the churches as the New Testament apostles
had. Now, the problem with that, I think, is that in the New Testament, the term apostle
clearly implied great authority and therefore it's unhelpful to use it today, even if one
uses it in a missionary's in a secondary sense of a church planter or whatever, because
the New Testament apostles clearly had authority to teach new doctrine and to teach morals
in an absolutely authoritative way. And when somebody claims to be an apostle today, it's
usually not very long before they're claiming the same kind of authority, and that is the
real problem. That is the real problem. When somebody today claims to have a kind of apostolic
authority, it very often needs to very serious problems because they exercise a kind of authority
which the New Testament clearly restricts to Peter and the others and Paul. And you can
run into the danger of people trying to teach new things and exercising tremendous power
over people's lives. The difficulty is the apostles claim in the New Testament that their
teaching has the authority of Christ himself and of the Old Testament scriptures. Many pastors
like that. We looked at 1 Corinthians 14, verse 37, and Paul says, "If anybody thinks
he's a prophet of Scripture, let him know that what I write is God's word. It's the
command of the Lord." Anybody who says that to you today without quoting Scripture and
has some serious problems in terms of the kind of power they're trying to exercise over
people's lives. And you have many other statements like that where the apostles speak of their
authority as being the same authority as the Old Testament scriptures so that there is
that practical problem also. Then that brings us to the other question and that is the question
of prophets today. There are all sorts of questions around the gift of prophecy today
which I think are important. First of all, what authority does the gift of prophecy have?
How we to understand the gift of prophecy in the New Testament? This is an important
question because there's a growing tendency in the church today to regard the gift of
prophecy as a being of very great importance and to regard the gift of prophecy as being
a direct word from God, often coming in the form, "Thus says the Lord," so that you
can have let's say a prayer meeting or church service, then somebody will stand up and instead
of saying after reading this passage of Scripture, I think this and this and this and this is
what the Scripture says. Somebody stands up and says, "Thus says the Lord, listen to
me," and then some sort of message follows which claims to be directly from God and yet
clearly or may not be something which is in the Scripture. There's a growing tendency
to exercise the gift of prophecy in that way today and also a growing tendency to see it
in an authoritative way. I remember recently seeing a letter from one leader in this country
who wrote, he said, "Why this is a man who feels he has the gift of prophecy and is
going around England exercising the gift," and he wrote in this letter, "I don't see
why evangelicals are making such a fuss about the authority of Scripture when we have prophecy
today, when we have God's word directly to us today." Now there are serious problems
when you begin moving in that direction because what one seems to be doing is setting Scripture
and prophecy side by side in terms of their importance and authority in the church. That's
always the difficulty. As soon as somebody prefaces something which isn't in the Bible
by saying, "Thus says the Lord," it comes across with the same sort of heaviness as
Isaiah did. When he said, "The word of the Lord came to me, thus and so," and he expected
people to listen to what he said and accepted as God's very word, or when Paul said, "What
I write is the word of the Lord," if somebody ignores that there to be ignored. Paul knew
that he had that authority from God. He was specially given it by God. But when somebody
just stands up and uses that kind of expression, it can be very, very confusing for the people
listening because they wonder, "Well, am I supposed to listen to that? Do I have to listen
to that?" as the voice of God to me, particularly if it's a prophecy which affects my life very
practically. An example I've come across was where somebody stood up. It was one of the
elders in the church in the States and said, "Thus says the Lord, our whole church must
move to Louisville, Kentucky." You know, so maybe whatever it happened to be. I'm just
plucking the name out of thin air. But they had to move hundreds of miles. Everybody went.
There were doctors who had been working in the community for years and people in schools,
lots of things. And this is a huge problem, and you have this. When somebody stands up
and says, "Thus says the Lord, this is what you must do because they're exercising a
tremendous control over people's lives." Now, what are we going to say as we look at the
New Testament? There are several ways the word the term prophecy is used in the New Testament.
The most important usage concerns the Old Testament prophets and their ministry. And
obviously, there are hundreds of examples in the Gospels and in the letters about the
Old Testament prophets. And it's summed up by the statement of Peter in 2 Peter 1 verses
20 and 21. He says, "Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture came
about by the prophets own interpretation. For prophecy never had its origin in the will
of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit." Now, that's
a summary of the New Testament's attitude towards the Old Testament prophets. But their
message was absolutely authoritative, authoritative because it never came by the will of man. It
came always from God. The holy man of God spoke as they were carried along by the Holy
Spirit. And that was 2 Peter 1 verses 20 and 21. Now, Jesus himself agreed completely with
such a view of the Old Testament prophets. You can think, for example, of his statement.
I referred to it in my sermon a couple of Sundays ago in Matthew 5, 17 through 18, where
Jesus says, "Not one little bit of all that the law and the prophets spoke will pass away."
And in Luke 24, 25, where Jesus rebukes the apostles, he says, "For being foolish and
slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken." So Jesus' attitude and the astute,
the rest of the New Testament to the Old Testament prophets, was that everything they prophesied
had total lasting and binding authority on the church. They had total lasting and binding
authority on the church, everything that they said. That's the New Testament's attitude
to the Old Testament prophets. It's therefore quite clear that when we come across a passage
like Ephesians 2, 20, the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and the prophets.
With Jesus himself as the cornerstone, it's quite clear that Paul is referring to the Old
Testament prophets and the New Testament apostles, the two groups of authors of Scripture. The
prophets, the authors of the Old Testament Scripture, the apostles, the authors of New
Testament Scripture, with Christ himself as the cornerstone.
Now such a passage as Ephesians 2, 20, should not be used, though it is used sometimes by
some, to try to give the New Testament gift of prophecy a binding authority on the church.
As we look at the gift of prophecy as it was exercised in the New Testament church,
it was clearly of a quite different nature from Old Testament prophecy. It's quite clearly
of a quite different nature from Old Testament prophecy. The Old Testament prophets were few
in number, were few in number who come from time to time over a period of many centuries.
Their word was binding when it was spoken and it's still binding today. Their message,
their writings were authoritative and with the authoritative writings of the New Testament
apostles, their writings are the foundation of the church because without the Scripture
there would be no church. The Old Testament prophets and the New Testament apostles are
the foundation of the church because without them there'd be no Bible. God gave them their
gift for the whole church of the future from their day right up until the second coming.
Now there is a contrast in the New Testament because when Paul writes to the Corinthians
he says that everybody should desire the gift of prophecy and be eager to prophesy. So we
have something very different from what you have in the Old Testament. They were few in
number, they came over a period of many centuries and their word was binding forever until the
second coming on the whole people of God. In the New Testament Paul says that everybody
be eager to prophesy 1 Corinthians 14 verse 1 and verse 39 and then Paul gives a definition
of prophecy. 1 Corinthians 14 verse 3 he says prophecy is speaking for the strengthening
encouragement and comfort of the church. 1 Corinthians 14 verse 3 Paul clearly understands
prophecy as speaking with the mind and that's a quote from him speaking with the mind when
he contrasts it with speaking in tongues which he calls a speaking with the spirit. That's
chapter 14 of 1 Corinthians 13 through 17. He clearly sees prophecy as a speaking with
the mind. In other words a human being thinking about what they're going to say. The prophet
is speaking with his mind and he contrasts it with tongues. The context of that passage
in verses 13 to 17 is the discussion of tongues and prophecy in the first 12 verses of chapter
14 of 1 Corinthians. In other words Paul does not understand the gift of prophecy as always
and necessarily being a message given directly by the spirit, thus says the Lord on every
occasion. Rather he understands prophecy as speaking with the mind for the practical
up building of the church as a gift which all believers ought to be eager to exercise
is to one another and I would say we all ought to be exercising it every day as we speak to
one another as we go around this place. In any church our desire should be to exercise
for gift of prophecy to one another all the time to build one another up as we speak to
apply the word of God practically to one another's lives. Now this does not mean the prophecy
should be seen as simply a natural human gift as opposed to some other supernatural divine
gift. As I said before the New Testament knows nothing of such a division between human
and divine or natural and supernatural. Then this follows on from this that the prophet,
so if we're talking about prophecy then it may involve the use of my mind that it will
be exercised in dependence upon the Holy Spirit as we should exercise any gift. But it means
then that the prophet is responsible for what he or she says. And I'm afraid sometimes
when somebody says, thus says the Lord, that it's a way of putting the responsibility for
what the individual says on God rather than taking the responsibility oneself. The prophet
must be seen as responsible for what he or she says. Now it's clear from Acts the gift
of prophecy may sometimes include a prediction of future events. You have some examples in
Acts the daughters of Philip and Agabus. Acts 21 verse 11 and Acts 20 verse 23 there is
a prophecy that there's going to be a famine. There is a prophecy that Paul will be imprisoned
when he goes to Jerusalem. So prophecy may include the prediction of future events. But
from Corinthians it is clear also that that is not always or even usually the case. And
then we must go on to say whether a prophecy is a prediction or what it will more often
be simply a practical word of wisdom, the prophecy is the responsibility of the person
who speaks it and does not have with it the absolute authority which the Old Testament
prophecies had. It does not have with it the absolute authority which the Old Testament
prophecies had. Why do I say that so strongly? Paul commands that prophecies must be weighed
and tested when they are given. 1 Corinthians 14, 29 and 32. Paul commands that all prophecies
had to be weighed and tested. In other words people had to think about it and say is this
right or isn't it? Just as we would with anybody says anything to us. Is it biblical
or isn't it? Is this what God wants or isn't it? They must be weighed and tested. Paul did
not expect his own words to be weighed and tested in that way nor did Jeremiah or Isaiah
when they prophesied because they spoke with authority. Paul repeatedly says that when
he spoke as an apostle he spoke with the authority of God himself and he didn't expect anybody
to weigh his words. He didn't have to bring them before the church to be weighed. That's
why Paul could write. Again 1 Corinthians 14, 37 if anybody thinks he's a prophet or spiritually
gifted, let him acknowledge that what I am writing to you is the Lord's command. So the
gift of prophecy in the New Testament church does not have a binding authority on people's
lives. Rather it was always subject to the apostolic word, the word of Scripture. It is
a very helpful illustration of that in the book of Acts. It says in Acts 20, 23 and 21
verse 11, but in every town prophecies are given that Paul will be imprisoned in Jerusalem.
Those who give the prophecies to Paul tell Paul that he should not go to Jerusalem. They
try to dissuade him. One of them binds Paul with chains and says don't go. They beg him
not to go with tears to Jerusalem. It's very interesting in the passages, Acts 21 verses
12 through 14. Paul does not question the accuracy of the prediction. He says in fact
the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every town that I'll be imprisoned when I go to Jerusalem.
Paul confirms the truth of the prediction. However, Paul does not regard the demand that
he should not go to Jerusalem as authoritative. Instead he insists that the Holy Spirit is
compelling him to go to Jerusalem, Acts 20 verse 22. In other words, what can we draw
from that? Paul had to make his own decision. Somebody may have made a prediction about
the future which was accurate. They drew the conclusion of Paul or not to go. Paul however
had to make up his own mind before the Lord as to what he had to do. We can draw some
conclusions from that for today. We ought to encourage the gift of prophecy. The gift
of prophecy might include predictions about the future or particular messages from the
Lord. You have an example in Acts 13 where it says the Holy Spirit said set aside Paul
and Barnabas for the ministry to which I've called them. Generally speaking, however,
prophecy will be words of practical encouragement and comfort which all of us should seek to
exercise. Then we must hold ourselves responsible and then finally prophecy must never be seen
as authoritative, never seen as binding on its hearers, and must never be used as such
by either the elders of a church, nor anybody else wanting to get their way in a church.
Somebody has a business to stand up and say, thus is the Lord, this is what you have got
to do and then insist that people do it and as it can clearly be shown from the Scripture
itself. When any prophecies are given they must be weighed and tested and the hearers
like Paul are not banned to evade them. Rather the hearers seek the Lord's face to confirm
for themselves what God's will is for their lives just as Paul did when he decided the
opposite of what the Prophet suggested. Finally again, only Scripture is binding. Only Scripture
is binding and nobody can claim to teach new things which are binding on anybody else's
life today. I'll stop there.
